question: In recent months, hundreds of thousands of EU citizens have supported the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Killing Games’, calling for regulation to protect consumer rights in the context of digital products, especially video games requiring a permanent connection to the internet.
The current practice of many large games publishers is to disable the server infrastructure some years after a title is first released, thereby preventing continued use of a legally acquired product.

Consumers are losing access to goods they have paid for, often without any compensation, while the companies are hiding behind licence agreements which, according to many experts, may conflict with existing EU consumer protection law.

The problem also concerns the inability to create private servers for games that are no longer supported, which limits users’ rights and negatively impacts the archiving of digital cultural heritage, which can be used by researchers, scientific institutions and video game history enthusiasts. 1.
Is the Commission planning to look into the problem of video games being disabled by publishers and its impact on consumer rights in the EU?
Does the Commission consider that the current licensing provisions, which allow access to a legally purchased product to be withdrawn, are compatible with EU consumer law?
Is the Commission considering proposing legislation to enable users to launch private servers for games which are no longer supported by the publisher?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.12.2025)

The Commission is aware of the European citizens’ initiative Stop killing Videogames. EU consumer protection legislation does not set specific duration for the supply of digital content/service but requires traders to supply it in accordance with the contract and consumer’s reasonable expectations.

Under Directive 2019/770/EU1 the discontinuation of the digital content/service by the trader sooner than what was contractually agreed or what the consumer may reasonably expect would constitute lack of conformity with the contract.

The trader can deviate from the objective requirements for conformity if it has specifically informed the consumer and the latter had expressly and separately accepted such deviation at the time of the conclusion of the contract. In the case of a lack of conformity, the consumer can terminate the contract causing the supplier’s obligation to refund part of the price paid.

Modern video game distribution models typically require users to agree to the terms and conditions governing their licensed use. Although these terms may differ between vendors, the licenses acquired are not perpetual. Such licensing conditions are part of the contract between the provider and consumer.
1 Directive (EU) 2019/770 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on certain aspects
concerning contracts for the supply of digital content and digital services, OJ L 136, 22.5.2019, p. 1-27.
